title: HCF & LCM
summary: Highest common factor and lowest common multiple — a small but near-guaranteed slot in CGL. Most questions are template word problems: greatest divisor with remainders (HCF of differences), least number with given remainders (LCM + r), bells, tiles and ratio pairs.

subtopics.title: HCF & LCM: definitions and core relations
subtopics.concept: The HCF is the largest number that divides every given number; the LCM is the smallest number that every given number divides. For two numbers, HCF times LCM equals their product. Numbers in a ratio are the ratio parts times the HCF.

formulas.name: LCM is a multiple of the HCF

tricks.title: Ratio split
tricks.body: Numbers in ratio a : b (co-prime parts) with HCF h are ha and hb. LCM = h times a times b; sum = h times (a plus b).

example.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 8 and their HCF is 9. Find their LCM.

tricks.title: Product divided by HCF
tricks.body: Given any two of product, HCF, LCM, the product relation settles the third in one division.

example.q: The product of two numbers is 2940 and their HCF is 14. Find the LCM.

tricks.title: Co-prime pairs from the quotient
tricks.body: For pair-count questions, divide the product by the square of the HCF, then count co-prime factor pairs of the result.

example.q: The product of two numbers is 216 and their HCF is 6. How many such pairs exist?

mistakes.wrong: Using HCF x LCM = product for three numbers.
mistakes.right: The relation holds for exactly two numbers only.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the co-prime pair (1, quotient) when counting pairs.
mistakes.right: That pair is always valid; include it in the count.

mistakes.wrong: Reading 'greatest number that divides' as an LCM question.
mistakes.right: 'Greatest that divides' is HCF; 'least that is divisible by' is LCM.

mistakes.wrong: Taking the HCF of a ratio pair to be the ratio itself.
mistakes.right: The HCF is the scale factor h; the ratio only gives the co-prime parts.

mistakes.wrong: Reporting an LCM that is not a multiple of the HCF.
mistakes.right: The LCM is always a multiple of the HCF; recheck the arithmetic.

subtopics.notes:
The HCF (highest common factor) is the largest number that divides each given number exactly. The LCM (lowest common multiple) is the smallest number that each given number divides exactly. For 12 and 18 the common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, so the HCF is 6; their multiples first meet at 36, so the LCM is 36.

### The size order
The HCF is never bigger than the smallest number. The LCM is never smaller than the largest number. So HCF $\le$ every number $\le$ LCM, for numbers of 1 or more. This order kills wrong options at sight.

> **Rule:** HCF $\le$ smallest number, and LCM $\ge$ largest number. An option breaking this order is wrong.

### The product relation
For exactly two numbers, HCF times LCM equals the product of the two numbers. Check on 12 and 18: $6 \times 36 = 216 = 12 \times 18$. The rule fails for three numbers, so never use it there. One common use is finding a missing number: other number $= \dfrac{\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM}}{\text{given number}}$.

> **Example:** HCF 15, LCM 225, one number 45. The other is $\dfrac{15 \times 225}{45} = 75$. Check: $\gcd(45, 75) = 15$ and $\text{LCM} = 225$.

### Numbers in a ratio
Numbers in ratio $a : b$ (parts co-prime) with HCF $h$ are $ha$ and $hb$. Then:
- LCM $= h \times a \times b$
- sum $= h(a + b)$
- difference $= h(b - a)$

Ratio 3 : 4 with HCF 6 gives 18 and 24, LCM $6 \times 12 = 72$, sum $6 \times 7 = 42$. Working backwards from an LCM: ratio 4 : 9 and LCM 252 give $h = \dfrac{252}{4 \times 9} = 7$, so the numbers are 28 and 63.

> **Tip:** Ratio and LCM given: divide the LCM by the product of the ratio parts. That quotient is the HCF.

### Co-prime and close numbers
Co-prime numbers have HCF 1, so their LCM is simply their product. Consecutive integers are always co-prime. The HCF also divides every difference of the numbers: two numbers 20 apart can never have HCF 12, because 12 does not divide 20.

One more standard shape: the HCF is $h$, and the other two factors of the LCM are $m$ and $n$ (co-prime). The numbers are $hm$ and $hn$, and the LCM is $hmn$. HCF 12 with other factors 5 and 7 gives numbers 60 and 84, and LCM $12 \times 35 = 420$.

> **Watch:** The LCM is always a multiple of the HCF. An LCM option that is not a multiple of the given HCF is wrong at sight.

### Counting pairs
A question may ask how many pairs of numbers have a given product $P$ and HCF $h$. Write the numbers as $ha$ and $hb$ with co-prime $a$ and $b$, so $ab = \dfrac{P}{h^2}$. The answer is the number of co-prime factor pairs of that quotient. The pair $(1, \text{quotient})$ counts as one pair. For product 216 with HCF 6: $\dfrac{216}{36} = 6$, and 6 has co-prime pairs $(1, 6)$ and $(2, 3)$, so 2 pairs exist: 6 with 36, and 12 with 18.

patterns.name: Find the HCF or LCM of small numbers directly
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks plainly for the HCF or LCM of two or three small numbers, with no story around it.
patterns.formula: \text{HCF} = \text{common primes, lowest powers}; \quad \text{LCM} = \text{all primes, highest powers}
steps: HCF: multiply the primes common to all numbers, at the lowest power of each.
LCM: multiply every prime that appears, at the highest power of each.
Sanity check: HCF at most the smallest number, LCM at least the largest.
patterns.why: A common divisor cannot use more of any prime than the poorest number holds; a common multiple needs the richest stock of every prime.

example.q: Find the LCM of 12, 15 and 20.
steps: Take the highest power of every prime: $2^2$, $3$, $5$.

patterns.name: HCF x LCM = product (two numbers)
patterns.howToSpot: Any two of product, HCF, LCM and one number are given, and a third value is asked.
steps: Confirm exactly two numbers are involved.
Write the product relation and fill in the three known values.
Divide to get the fourth value.
Check: the HCF must divide the LCM, and the HCF must divide both numbers.
patterns.why: Writing $a = ha'$ and $b = hb'$ with co-prime parts, the LCM is $ha'b'$, so HCF times LCM equals $ab$.

example.q: The HCF of two numbers is 12, their LCM is 240, and one number is 48. Find the other number.

patterns.name: Numbers in a given ratio, HCF or LCM known
patterns.howToSpot: Two numbers are in a ratio and the HCF or LCM is given; a sum, difference or the numbers themselves are asked.
steps: Cancel the ratio to co-prime parts $m : n$ first.
HCF given: the numbers are $hm$ and $hn$.
LCM given: $h = \dfrac{\text{LCM}}{mn}$, then the numbers are $hm$ and $hn$.
Answer what is asked: sum, difference, product or the numbers.
patterns.why: The ratio fixes only the shape of the pair; the HCF is the scale factor that stretches it.

example.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 7 and their LCM is 700. Find their sum.

patterns.name: HCF given with the other factors of the LCM
patterns.howToSpot: The HCF is given together with the two leftover factors of the LCM, and the numbers are asked.
steps: The numbers are HCF times the first other factor, and HCF times the second.
The two other factors must be co-prime; otherwise the data is impossible.
If asked, the LCM is HCF times the product of the two factors.
patterns.why: The LCM equals the HCF times the leftover co-prime parts, by the structure of the two ideas.

example.q: The HCF of two numbers is 17 and the other two factors of their LCM are 11 and 16. Find the greater number.

patterns.name: Co-prime, consecutive and property questions
patterns.howToSpot: The word co-prime or consecutive appears, or a pair must be tested for being co-prime.
steps: Co-prime with LCM given: divide the LCM by the given number to get the other.
Testing a pair for co-prime: check for any common factor above 1.
Difference checks: a common factor must divide the difference of the pair.
patterns.why: With no common prime between them, nothing cancels, so the LCM is the plain product.

example.q: The LCM of two co-prime numbers is 312 and one of them is 13. Find the other number.

revision: Two numbers: $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = ab$. Three numbers: no such rule.
Co-prime numbers: HCF 1, LCM product. Consecutive integers are co-prime.
Ratio $a : b$ with HCF $h$: numbers $ha$, $hb$; LCM $hab$; sum $h(a + b)$.
HCF divides every difference; LCM is a multiple of the HCF.
Other factors $m$, $n$ of the LCM: numbers $hm$, $hn$; LCM $hmn$.
Pair count: co-prime factor pairs of product $\div h^2$.

subtopics.title: Finding HCF & LCM (incl. fractions and decimals)
subtopics.concept: Prime factorisation reads HCF from the lowest powers and LCM from the highest powers. Long division finds the HCF of two big numbers fast, and one division gives the LCM. Fractions swap the rules: HCF of tops over LCM of bottoms.

tricks.title: Row of prime powers
tricks.body: Write each number as a row of prime powers in a small grid. LCM reads the column maxima, HCF the common minima. Three numbers take under thirty seconds.

example.q: Find the LCM of 18, 24 and 30.

tricks.title: Cross rule for fractions
tricks.body: HCF of fractions: HCF of tops over LCM of bottoms. LCM of fractions: LCM of tops over HCF of bottoms.

example.q: Find the HCF of 3/4, 5/6 and 7/8.

tricks.title: Shift the decimal point
tricks.body: Multiply by the power of 10 that clears every decimal, solve as integers, then shift the point back by the same number of places.

example.q: Find the LCM of 0.2, 0.25 and 0.4.

mistakes.wrong: Taking the HCF of fractions as HCF of tops over HCF of bottoms.
mistakes.right: The denominator of the HCF is the LCM of the bottoms.

mistakes.wrong: Skipping the reduction of fractions before the cross rule.
mistakes.right: Reduce every fraction to lowest terms first.

mistakes.wrong: Giving the LCM the lowest powers and the HCF the highest.
mistakes.right: HCF reads minima, LCM reads maxima.

mistakes.wrong: Returning a whole-number answer for a decimals question.
mistakes.right: The scale factor of 10 must be divided back out at the end.

mistakes.wrong: Stopping long division at the first zero remainder divisor shown.
mistakes.right: The HCF is the last non-zero divisor, not any earlier divisor.

subtopics.notes:
Every HCF or LCM question starts by picking a method. Small numbers yield to prime factorisation, two big numbers to long division, fractions to the cross rule, and decimals to shifting the point. For 24, 36 and 50: $24 = 2^3 \times 3$, $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$, $50 = 2 \times 5^2$, so the HCF is $2$ and the LCM is $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 1800$.

### Prime factorisation
Write each number as a product of primes, one row per number in a small table.
- HCF: multiply the primes common to every number, each at its lowest power.
- LCM: multiply every prime that appears, each at its highest power.

Reading the table column by column does the work: column minima give the HCF, column maxima give the LCM. If no prime is common to all numbers, the HCF is 1.

> **Rule:** HCF takes the lowest powers of common primes; LCM takes the highest powers of all primes.

### Long division for two big numbers
Divide the bigger number by the smaller. Then divide the old divisor by the remainder. Repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero divisor is the HCF. For 432 and 180: $432 = 2 \times 180 + 72$, then $180 = 2 \times 72 + 36$, then $72 = 2 \times 36 + 0$. The HCF is 36. The LCM then falls out as $\dfrac{432 \times 180}{36} = 2160$.

For three numbers, chain the process: HCF of the first two, then HCF of that result with the third.

> **Tip:** After the HCF, get the LCM as product divided by HCF. Never multiply the numbers out fully first; cancel the HCF first.

### Numbers already in prime-power form
When the question hands you numbers like $2^4 \times 3 \times 5$ and $2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5^2$, skip factorising. HCF: lowest power of each prime, here $2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$. LCM: highest power of each prime, here $2^4 \times 3^3 \times 5^2 = 10800$. Multiply out only at the end.

### Fractions: the cross rule
$$\text{HCF} = \dfrac{\text{HCF of numerators}}{\text{LCM of denominators}}, \qquad \text{LCM} = \dfrac{\text{LCM of numerators}}{\text{HCF of denominators}}$$
The two rules mirror each other, so swap them deliberately. HCF of $\dfrac{2}{3}, \dfrac{8}{9}, \dfrac{10}{27}$ is $\dfrac{\gcd(2, 8, 10)}{\text{LCM}(3, 9, 27)} = \dfrac{2}{27}$.

> **Watch:** Reduce every fraction to lowest terms before applying the cross rule; a reducible fraction corrupts both lists.

### Decimals: shift the point
Count the largest number of decimal places, multiply everything by that power of 10, solve as whole numbers, then shift the point back. LCM of $0.15, 0.20, 0.45$: work with $15, 20, 45$, whose LCM is 180, so the answer is 1.80.

> **Example:** Check by dividing: $1.80 \div 0.15 = 12$, $1.80 \div 0.20 = 9$, $1.80 \div 0.45 = 4$. All whole, so 1.80 is right.

### Choosing a method fast
Small numbers: factorise mentally. Two big numbers: long division. Prime-power form: read minima and maxima. Fractions: cross rule. Decimals: clear the point, restore it at the end.

patterns.name: HCF by successive (long) division
patterns.howToSpot: Two or three larger numbers appear and the HCF is asked; the numbers are too big to factorise comfortably.
patterns.formula: \gcd(a, b): \text{ divide, then divide the divisor by the remainder; the last non-zero divisor is the HCF}
steps: Divide the bigger number by the smaller and note the remainder.
Divide the previous divisor by that remainder.
The last non-zero divisor is the HCF; for a third number, chain once more.
patterns.why: Every common divisor of the two numbers also divides each remainder, so the process keeps the common divisors while the numbers shrink.

example.q: Find the HCF of 1617 and 903 by successive division.

patterns.name: HCF and LCM from prime-power form
patterns.howToSpot: The numbers arrive as prime products like 2 cubed times 3 squared times 5, and HCF or LCM is asked.
steps: List every prime that appears in any number.
HCF: take the smallest exponent of each prime across all numbers; skip a prime missing from any number.
LCM: take the largest exponent of each prime anywhere.
Multiply out only at the end.
patterns.why: The HCF must fit inside every number; the LCM must contain every number.

example.q: Find the LCM of the numbers $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$, $2^2 \times 3^3 \times 7$ and $2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2$.

patterns.name: HCF and LCM of fractions (cross rule)
patterns.howToSpot: A list of fractions like 2/3, 8/9, 10/27 is given and the HCF or LCM of the fractions is asked.
steps: Reduce each fraction to lowest terms.
For the HCF: HCF of the tops over LCM of the bottoms.
For the LCM: LCM of the tops over HCF of the bottoms.
Check: every fraction divided by the HCF is whole; the LCM divided by every fraction is whole.
patterns.why: Putting all fractions over the LCM of the denominators turns them into whole numbers, and the ordinary rules on those integers give the cross rule.

example.q: Find the LCM of 2/3, 8/9 and 10/27.

patterns.name: HCF and LCM of decimals
patterns.howToSpot: Decimal values like 0.63, 1.05 and 2.1 are given, and the answer carries a decimal point.
patterns.formula: \text{scale by } 10^k \to \text{integer HCF or LCM} \to \text{scale back by } 10^k
steps: Count the largest number of decimal places among the values.
Multiply every value by that power of 10 so all become integers.
Find the HCF or LCM of the integers.
Divide the result by the same power of 10.
patterns.why: A common scale factor multiplies both HCF and LCM by itself, so undo it at the end.

example.q: Find the HCF of 0.63, 1.05 and 2.1.

patterns.name: LCM of two large numbers via the HCF
patterns.howToSpot: The LCM of two numbers too large to factorise is asked directly, or the HCF was already found.
steps: Find the HCF first, by long division.
Divide one number by the HCF.
Multiply the quotient by the other number.
Never multiply the two big numbers first; cancel the HCF before multiplying.
patterns.why: The product of two numbers equals HCF times LCM, so dividing by the HCF leaves the LCM without a huge multiplication.

example.q: Find the LCM of 1617 and 903.

revision: HCF: common primes, lowest powers. LCM: every prime, highest powers.
Long division: last non-zero divisor is the HCF; LCM $= \dfrac{ab}{\text{HCF}}$.
Three or more numbers: chain the HCF pairwise.
Prime-power form: read minima and maxima straight off.
Fractions: HCF of tops over LCM of bottoms, and the mirror for LCM.
Decimals: clear the point, solve, restore the same number of places.

subtopics.title: Standard word problems (tiles, bells, groups, divisible numbers)
subtopics.concept: Word problems here sort into two families. Anything 'greatest that divides' is an HCF; anything 'least that is divisible by' is an LCM. Remainders shift the number first: subtract them for the HCF, add them back for the LCM.

formulas.name: Remainder is divisor minus c
formulas.tex: r_i = d_i - c \Rightarrow N = \text{LCM} \times k - c

tricks.title: Subtract remainders, then HCF
tricks.body: For 'greatest number dividing a and b leaving remainders r1 and r2', the answer is the HCF of (a - r1) and (b - r2).

example.q: Find the greatest number which divides 1000 and 750 leaving remainders 4 and 6.

tricks.title: LCM plus r
tricks.body: For 'least number leaving remainder r with each divisor', add r to the LCM of the divisors.

example.q: Find the least number which when divided by 12, 16 and 24 leaves remainder 8 in each case.

tricks.title: Bells: add the LCM to the clock
tricks.body: Convert all intervals to one unit, take the LCM, and add it to the given start time.

example.q: Four lights blink every 12, 15, 18 and 30 seconds and blink together at noon. When do they next blink together?

mistakes.wrong: Adding the remainder in a 'greatest number that divides' question.
mistakes.right: That family needs the HCF of the numbers minus their remainders.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing metres with centimetres, or minutes with seconds.
mistakes.right: Convert all measurements to one unit before the HCF or LCM.

mistakes.wrong: Reporting LCM + r when a larger value was demanded by a bound.
mistakes.right: Fit LCM times k plus r into the stated range; the least uses k = 1.

mistakes.wrong: Using the HCF where the question says 'divisible by all'.
mistakes.right: 'Divisible by all' is an LCM question; 'divides all' is HCF.

mistakes.wrong: Counting the starting moment in a bells question without checking the wording.
mistakes.right: Divide the window by the LCM; add 1 only if the start counts.

subtopics.notes:
Every word problem in this topic is a dressed-up HCF or LCM question. The fastest first step is to name the family: 'greatest number that divides' means HCF, 'least number divisible by' means LCM. For bells that toll together every 6, 8 and 12 minutes, the gap is $\text{LCM} = 24$ minutes.

### The template table
| Question wording | Tool |
|---|---|
| Greatest number that divides a, b, c | HCF |
| Least number divisible by a, b, c | LCM |
| Largest tile, rod or biggest equal group | HCF |
| Bells or lights together again | LCM |
| Least number, remainder r with every divisor | LCM + r |
| Greatest number, remainder r with every divisor | HCF of (number - r) |

> **Tip:** 'Greatest' pairs with HCF; 'least' pairs with LCM. Fix the family first, then the arithmetic is short.

### Divides with remainders
'Find the greatest number which divides 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8.' The divisor must divide $70 - 5 = 65$ and $125 - 8 = 117$, so it divides their HCF. $\gcd(65, 117) = 13$. Check: $70 = 5 \times 13 + 5$ and $125 = 9 \times 13 + 8$.

> **Rule:** Subtract each remainder from its number, then take the HCF. The answer must exceed every remainder.

### Same remainder with every divisor
If N leaves remainder r with every divisor, then $N - r$ is divisible by all of them. The least such N is LCM + r. For divisors 9, 12, 15 with remainder 5: $\text{LCM} = 180$, so $N = 185$.

### Remainders that differ by a constant
When each remainder is the same amount c below its divisor, add c instead. For divisors 6, 9, 12 with remainders 5, 8, 11: each remainder is divisor $- 1$, so $N + 1$ is a common multiple. $N = \text{LCM}(6, 9, 12) - 1 = 36 - 1 = 35$. Check: $35 \bmod 6 = 5$, $35 \bmod 9 = 8$, $35 \bmod 12 = 11$.

> **Watch:** Each remainder must be smaller than its divisor. A remainder bigger than its divisor means the working stopped one step early.

### Bells, lights and laps
Convert every interval to one unit, then take the LCM. Buses leaving every 10, 15 and 20 minutes together at 6 a.m. meet again after $\text{LCM} = 60$ minutes, at 7 a.m. To count meetings inside a window, divide the window by the LCM; add 1 only if the starting moment itself counts.

### Tiles, rods, vessels and groups
The largest square tile has side $\gcd(L, W)$ in the same units; the tile count is $\dfrac{L \times W}{h^2}$. The longest rod cut from planks of 42 cm and 49 cm has length $\gcd = 7$ cm, giving $6 + 7 = 13$ pieces. Equal groups of people: the group size is the HCF of the counts.

> **Example:** A hall is 8.4 m by 5.6 m, so 840 cm by 560 cm. The largest square tile has side $\gcd(840, 560) = 280$ cm, and $\dfrac{840 \times 560}{280^2} = 6$ tiles.

### Units first
Convert everything before computing: 2 m 40 cm is 240 cm, and 3 hours is 180 minutes. Mixed units are the number-one error here, because the HCF or LCM changes with the unit.

patterns.name: Greatest number dividing with given remainders
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the greatest number which divides two or three numbers leaving stated remainders.
steps: Subtract each remainder from its number; the divisor divides each difference.
Take the HCF of the differences.
Check the answer exceeds every remainder.
patterns.why: The unknown divisor divides each N minus r, so it is a common factor, and the greatest one is the HCF.

example.q: Find the greatest number which divides 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8.

patterns.name: Least number leaving the same remainder (LCM + r)
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the least number which when divided by several divisors leaves the same remainder each time.
steps: Take the LCM of the divisors.
Add the remainder r for the least value.
With a bound (four-digit, above 1000), pick k so that LCM x k + r fits.
patterns.why: N minus r must be a common multiple of all divisors, and the least positive one is the LCM.

example.q: Find the least number which when divided by 9, 12 and 15 leaves remainder 5 in each case.

patterns.name: Remainder is divisor minus c each time
patterns.howToSpot: The remainders differ, but each one sits a fixed amount below its own divisor.
patterns.formula: r_i = d_i - c \Rightarrow N = \text{LCM}(d_1, d_2, \ldots) \times k - c
steps: Subtract each remainder from its divisor; confirm the same value c every time.
Then N + c is divisible by every divisor.
The least N is LCM minus c.
patterns.why: Adding c repairs every division to an exact one, so N + c is a common multiple.

example.q: Find the least number which when divided by 5, 6 and 8 leaves remainders 4, 5 and 7.

patterns.name: Bells, lights and laps meeting again
patterns.howToSpot: Events repeat at different intervals, start together, and the question asks when they next coincide or how often.
steps: Convert every interval to the same unit.
The LCM of the intervals is the gap between coincidences.
Add the gap to the start time, or divide the window by it to count meetings.
Check the wording for whether the starting moment counts.
patterns.why: Two repeating events coincide exactly at common multiples of their periods, and the first one is the LCM.

example.q: Three bells toll every 6, 8 and 12 minutes and toll together at 7 a.m. When do they next toll together?

patterns.name: Largest tile, rod, vessel or equal group
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the largest square tile, longest equal rod, biggest vessel, or biggest identical groups.
steps: Convert all measurements to one unit.
The HCF of the dimensions or counts gives the size.
Divide the total by the HCF for the count of tiles, pieces or groups.
patterns.why: The tile or rod must fit each dimension a whole number of times, so it is a common divisor; the largest is the HCF.

example.q: A hall is 8.4 m long and 5.6 m wide. Find the largest square tile that paves it exactly, and the number of tiles.

revision: 'Greatest that divides' $\to$ HCF; 'least divisible by' $\to$ LCM.
Divides with remainders: subtract remainders, take HCF.
Same remainder r, least value: LCM $+ r$.
Each remainder $= $ divisor $- c$: least value LCM $- c$.
Bells and laps: LCM of intervals, then add to the clock.
Tiles and rods: HCF of dimensions; count $=$ area $\div h^2$ or total $\div h$.
Convert units before anything else.

subtopics.title: Two-step LCM/HCF cases (extra condition, N-digit bounds)
subtopics.concept: Harder questions chain one extra condition onto an LCM or HCF. Write N = LCM x k + r and let the condition pin down k, or rebuild numbers as h times co-prime parts from the HCF and LCM.

tricks.title: Test k until it clicks
tricks.body: Once N = LCM x k + r is written, only k remains. Test k = 1, 2, 3 against the extra condition; small values click fast.

example.q: Find the least number which leaves remainder 1 with 3, 5 and 7, and is divisible by 8.

tricks.title: n-digit multiple scan
tricks.body: For the least n-digit multiple, divide the smallest n-digit number by the LCM and step up to the next multiple. For the greatest, subtract the remainder from the largest n-digit number.

example.q: Find the least three-digit number exactly divisible by 9 and 12.

tricks.title: Sum or difference picks the pair
tricks.body: With HCF, LCM and a sum or difference given, list co-prime pairs of LCM / HCF and match h times the parts to the sum.

example.q: Two numbers have HCF 6, LCM 180 and sum 66. Find the numbers.

mistakes.wrong: Answering LCM + r when an extra condition forces a larger multiple.
mistakes.right: Fit N = LCM x k + r through the extra condition and take the smallest k that works.

mistakes.wrong: Listing factor pairs of LCM / HCF without checking co-primality.
mistakes.right: Only co-prime pairs are possible; drop the rest before matching the sum.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting the pair (1, M) when counting possibilities.
mistakes.right: That pair is always co-prime and always counts.

mistakes.wrong: Counting (a, b) and (b, a) as two pairs.
mistakes.right: Order does not matter; count each pair once with a at most b.

mistakes.wrong: Skipping the check that the HCF divides the sum or difference.
mistakes.right: The HCF must divide both numbers, so it divides their sum and difference too.

subtopics.notes:
The harder questions in this topic add one extra condition to a plain LCM or HCF setup. The master frame is $N = L \times k + r$, where $L$ is the LCM of the divisors. For divisors 5 and 6 with remainder 2: $L = 30$, so $N = 30k + 2$, giving 32, 62, 92, and so on.

### The master frame
$k = 1$ gives the least positive value; larger k walks up the same family. Any extra condition, such as divisibility by one more number or a digit bound, simply selects k.

> **Rule:** Write $N = L \times k + r$ first. Then fit the extra condition onto k.

### An extra divisibility condition
Test $k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ until $Lk + r$ satisfies the condition. For 'N leaves remainder 2 with 5 and 6, and N is divisible by 7': $N = 30k + 2$. Trying k gives 32, 62, 122, 152, 182, and $182 = 7 \times 26$ works. So $N = 182$.

### Least and greatest n-digit numbers
Multiples of $L$ are the candidates. Least four-digit multiple of 60: $1000 = 16 \times 60 + 40$, so add $60 - 40 = 20$ to reach 1020. Greatest works from the top: divide 99,999 by 60, subtract the remainder, and land on the greatest multiple under the bound.

> **Tip:** Step up from 10, 100, 1000 for the least; step down from 9, 99, 999 for the greatest. With a remainder r, fit $Lk + r$ inside the range instead of plain multiples.

### Rebuilding numbers from HCF and LCM
Numbers with HCF $h$ are $ha$ and $hb$ with co-prime parts, and $ab = \dfrac{\text{LCM}}{h}$. With HCF 4 and LCM 48: $ab = 12$, whose co-prime pairs are $(1, 12)$ and $(3, 4)$. A given sum picks the pair: sum 28 needs $a + b = 7$, so the parts are 3 and 4 and the numbers are 12 and 16.

> **Watch:** List only co-prime factor pairs. The pair $(2, 6)$ for $ab = 12$ is impossible, because the numbers would share an extra factor 2.

### Counting possible pairs
Count the co-prime factor pairs of $ab$, and remember the pair $(1, ab)$. Product 1764 with HCF 14 gives $ab = \dfrac{1764}{14^2} = 9$, and 9 has the single co-prime pair $(1, 9)$: the numbers must be 14 and 126. Count each unordered pair once, with the smaller part first, so $(1, 9)$ and $(9, 1)$ are the same pair.

### Sanity checks that catch slips
Two quick filters catch most slips in this subtopic. First, the HCF must divide the LCM, both numbers, and their sum and difference. Second, every rebuilt pair must multiply back to the product and carry the stated HCF. Run both checks before marking the answer.

### The same unknown remainder
When no remainder is given but it is the same for all numbers, the divisor divides every pairwise difference. For 51, 123 and 171: the differences are 72, 48 and 120, and $\gcd(72, 48, 120) = 24$. The common remainder is $51 \bmod 24 = 3$, the same for all three.

> **Example:** Check: $123 = 5 \times 24 + 3$ and $171 = 7 \times 24 + 3$. Both leave remainder 3, so 24 is right.

patterns.name: Least or greatest n-digit number divisible by a set
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the least or greatest number of a given digit count divisible by several divisors.
patterns.formula: \text{least: next multiple of } L \text{ at or above } 10^{n-1}; \quad \text{greatest: } 10^n - 1 - \left((10^n - 1) \bmod L\right)
steps: Take $L$ as the LCM of the divisors.
Least: divide the smallest n-digit number by $L$ and step up to the next multiple.
Greatest: divide the largest n-digit number by $L$ and subtract the remainder.
With a remainder r in the question, fit $Lk + r$ inside the range instead.
patterns.why: Multiples of the LCM are exactly the numbers divisible by every divisor; the digit bounds only pick where to stop.

example.q: Find the greatest five-digit number exactly divisible by 12, 15 and 20.

patterns.name: LCM + r with an extra condition
patterns.howToSpot: An LCM plus remainder question carries one more filter, such as divisibility by another number or a digit bound.
patterns.formula: N = Lk + r, \qquad \text{smallest } k \text{ meeting the condition wins}
steps: Write $N = L \times k + r$ with $L$ the LCM of the divisors.
With an n-digit bound, start k just above the bound minus r, divided by L.
patterns.why: N minus r is a multiple of L by construction; the extra condition only chooses which multiple.

example.q: Find the least number which leaves remainder 3 with 6, 7 and 8, and is divisible by 5.

patterns.name: Rebuild numbers from HCF and LCM; count pairs
patterns.howToSpot: HCF and LCM are given with a sum, difference or bound; find the numbers, or count the possible pairs.
steps: List factor pairs of $ab$ and keep only co-prime pairs.
Use the given sum or difference to pick the pair; the numbers are $ha$ and $hb$.
To count pairs, count the surviving co-prime pairs.
patterns.why: Two numbers with HCF h are h times two co-prime parts, and those parts must multiply to LCM divided by h.

example.q: The HCF and LCM of two numbers are 6 and 36. How many pairs of numbers fit?
steps: Pairs: 6 with 36, and 12 with 18. That is 2 pairs.

patterns.name: Greatest number dividing with the same unknown remainder
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the greatest number dividing a, b, c and leaving the same remainder in each case, with no remainder given.
steps: Take the pairwise differences of the numbers.
The HCF of the differences is the greatest such divisor.
The common remainder is any number mod that HCF; confirm it is the same for all.
patterns.why: If two numbers leave the same remainder, their difference is exactly divisible by the divisor, so it divides every difference.

example.q: Find the greatest number which divides 61, 109 and 133 leaving the same remainder in each case.

patterns.name: LCM + r inside a digit bound
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the least (or greatest) number of a given digit count leaving remainder r with several divisors.
steps: Write $N = L \times k + r$ with $L$ the LCM of the divisors.
Least n-digit: take the smallest k with $Lk + r$ at or above the smallest n-digit number.
Greatest n-digit: take the largest k with $Lk + r$ at or below the largest n-digit number.
Check the remainder with every divisor.
patterns.why: The family of valid numbers is exactly LCM multiples plus r; the digit bound selects the first or last member.

example.q: Find the least four-digit number which leaves remainder 3 when divided by 6, 7 and 8.

revision: Master frame: $N = L \times k + r$; extra conditions only choose $k$.
Least n-digit multiple: step up from $10 \ldots 0$; greatest: step down from $99 \ldots 9$.
Numbers from HCF and LCM: $ab = \text{LCM} \div h$, co-prime parts only.
Pair count: co-prime factor pairs of LCM $\div h$ (or product $\div h^2$).
Same unknown remainder: HCF of pairwise differences.
Common remainder check: any number mod the answer, same value for all.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Greatest number dividing with same/known remainders (HCF of differences)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the greatest number which divides x, y, z leaving remainders a, b, c' (remainders equal or different).
pyqPatterns.approach: Subtract each remainder from its number and take the HCF of the results — the divisor divides every (number − remainder) exactly. If the remainders are not even mentioned, take the HCF of the pairwise differences of the numbers instead.

example.q: Find the greatest number which divides 82, 150 and 233 leaving remainders 4, 7 and 12 respectively.
example.solution: Subtract: 78, 143, 221. HCF = 13 (each is a multiple of 13).

pyqPatterns.pattern: Least number leaving the same remainder (LCM + r)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the least number which when divided by a, b, c leaves remainder r in each case.'
pyqPatterns.approach: Take the LCM of the divisors and add r. With an extra condition (n-digit bound, or divisible by p), write N = LCM·k + r and fit the condition by testing k = 1, 2, 3, …

example.q: Find the least number which when divided by 8, 12, 15 and 20 leaves remainder 4 in each case.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Remainder is (divisor − c) each time (LCM − c)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The remainders look different, but each is a fixed amount less than its divisor — e.g. remainders 2, 3, 4 with divisors 3, 4, 5.
pyqPatterns.approach: Check that divisor − remainder is the same number c in every case. Then N + c is divisible by all divisors, so the least N is LCM − c (and other values are LCM·k − c).

example.q: Find the least number which when divided by 6, 9 and 12 leaves remainders 5, 8 and 11 respectively.
example.solution: Each remainder is 1 less than its divisor: N = LCM − 1 = 36 − 1 = 35.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Two numbers are in ratio m : n and their HCF (or LCM) is …' — then sum, difference, product or LCM is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cancel the ratio to co-prime parts m, n. Numbers are h·m and h·n where h is the HCF. From the LCM: h = LCM/(m·n). Then compute whatever is asked — sum = h(m + n), difference = h(n − m), LCM = h·m·n.

example.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 7 and their LCM is 140. Find the numbers.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two of {product, HCF, LCM, one number} are given; find the fourth, or 'how many pairs are possible'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use HCF × LCM = product (two numbers only). For pair counts, split product ÷ HCF² (or LCM ÷ HCF) into co-prime factor pairs, always including the pair (1, M).

example.q: The product of two numbers is 2160 and their HCF is 12. Find their LCM.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Events repeating at fixed intervals start together; asked when they next coincide, or how many times inside a time window.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert all intervals to one unit, take the LCM — that is the coincidence gap. Add it to the start time for 'when next'; divide the window by it for 'how many times' (add 1 only if the start itself counts).

example.q: Three bells toll at intervals of 9, 12 and 15 minutes, together at 8 a.m. When do they next toll together?

pyqPatterns.pattern: Largest tile / rod / measure / group size (HCF)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Paving with the largest square tiles, cutting equal planks of greatest length, the biggest vessel filling containers, biggest equal groups.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert all measurements to the same unit and take the HCF. Then count: tiles = (L × B)/side², pieces = total length ÷ HCF, groups = count ÷ HCF.

example.q: What is the largest vessel that can fill 144 L, 180 L and 240 L containers exactly?

pyqPatterns.pattern: Greatest / least n-digit number with LCM or remainder conditions
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the greatest four-digit number divisible by …' / 'least five-digit number which divided by … leaves remainder …'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Take the LCM first. Least: step up from 10…0 to the next multiple (fit N = LCM·k + r into the range if a remainder is given). Greatest: reduce 99…9 by its remainder.

example.q: Find the least five-digit number exactly divisible by 32, 36, 40, 45 and 48.

pyqPatterns.pattern: HCF / LCM of fractions or decimals
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A list like 2/3, 8/9, 10/27, or decimals like 0.54, 1.8, 7.2.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fractions: HCF = (HCF of numerators)/(LCM of denominators); LCM is the mirror image. Decimals: multiply everything by the same power of 10 to clear the point, solve as integers, then put the point back.

example.q: Find the HCF of 0.54, 1.8 and 7.2.

solvedExamples.q: The HCF of two numbers is 145 and their LCM is 2175. If one number is 725, find the other number.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 725 = 145 × 5, so the other must be 145 × 3 = 435 because LCM ÷ HCF = 2175/145 = 15 = 5 × 3 with (5, 3) co-prime.

solvedExamples.q: Find the greatest number which when dividing 85 and 72 leaves remainders 1 and 2 respectively.
solvedExamples.solution:
The required number divides 85 − 1 = 84 and 72 − 2 = 70 exactly.
$84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$, $70 = 2 \times 5 \times 7$ ⇒ HCF $= 14$.
Check: $85 = 6 \times 14 + 1$ ✓, $72 = 5 \times 14 + 2$ ✓.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Subtract the remainders, take the HCF: gcd(84, 70) = 14. (Option 83/17 ignore one condition; 8 divides both but is not the greatest.)

solvedExamples.solution:
HCF of numerators: $\gcd(2, 8, 10) = 2$.
LCM of denominators: $\text{LCM}(3, 9, 27) = 27$.
Answer: $\frac{2}{27}$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Cross rule: HCF of tops / LCM of bottoms = 2/27.

solvedExamples.q: Find the least number of square tiles required to pave a hall 15 m 17 cm long and 9 m 2 cm broad.
solvedExamples.solution:
Convert: 15 m 17 cm = 1517 cm, 9 m 2 cm = 902 cm.
$\gcd(1517, 902) = 41$ (since $1517 = 37 \times 41$ and $902 = 22 \times 41$).
Tile size 41 cm × 41 cm; number of tiles $= \frac{1517 \times 902}{41 \times 41} = 37 \times 22 = 814$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Factor both: 1517 = 37 × 41, 902 = 22 × 41 ⇒ side 41, tiles = 37 × 22 = 814. (902 is the breadth — a trap.)

solvedExamples.q: The HCF and LCM of two numbers are 5 and 495 respectively. If their sum is 100, find their difference.
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the numbers be $5a$ and $5b$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$.
$5a \times 5b = 5 \times 495$ ⇒ $ab = 99$.
Co-prime pairs of 99 = 9 × 11: (1, 99) and (9, 11).
Sum: $5(a + b) = 100$ ⇒ $a + b = 20$ ⇒ $(a, b) = (9, 11)$.
Numbers: 45 and 55 ⇒ difference **10**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: LCM/HCF = 99 = 9 × 11 (the only co-prime pair with a workable sum). Numbers 45 & 55 → difference 10.
solvedExamples.pattern: reconstruct numbers from HCF and LCM

practice.q: What is the HCF of 96 and 404?
practice.solution:
$96 = 2^5 \times 3$, $404 = 2^2 \times 101$.
Common prime with lowest power: $2^2 = 4$.
practice.shortcut: 404 = 4 × 101 and 101 is prime, so the HCF is gcd(96, 4) = 4.

practice.q: The LCM of 12, 15 and 20 is:
practice.shortcut: 60 is the only option divisible by all three (120 works but is not the least).

practice.q: The product of two numbers is 1600 and their HCF is 5. The LCM of the numbers is:
practice.solution: $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = $ product ⇒ $\text{LCM} = \frac{1600}{5} = 320$.
practice.shortcut: 1600 ÷ 5 = 320. Quick check: LCM must be a multiple of HCF 5 ✓.

practice.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 2 : 3 and their LCM is 48. The sum of the numbers is:
practice.solution:
Let the numbers be $2k$ and $3k$ (co-prime parts).
LCM $= 6k = 48$ ⇒ $k = 8$.
Numbers: 16 and 24 ⇒ sum $= 40$.
practice.shortcut: LCM of a 2:3 pair is 6k = 48 ⇒ k = 8 ⇒ 16 + 24 = 40.

practice.q: Find the greatest number which divides 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8 respectively.
practice.solution:
Required number divides 70 − 5 = 65 and 125 − 8 = 117.
$65 = 5 \times 13$, $117 = 9 \times 13$ ⇒ HCF $= 13$.
practice.shortcut: gcd(65, 117) = 13. (Options 65 and 117 are the numbers themselves after subtraction — a classic trap.)

practice.q: Three bells toll at intervals of 9, 12 and 15 minutes respectively. If they toll together at 8 a.m., at what time will they toll together next?
practice.shortcut: LCM of 9, 12, 15 is 180 min = 3 h ⇒ 11 a.m.

practice.q: The HCF of two numbers is 29, and the other two factors of their LCM are 15 and 13. The larger of the two numbers is:
practice.solution:
The numbers are $29 \times 15 = 435$ and $29 \times 13 = 377$ (15 and 13 are co-prime).
Their LCM is $29 \times 15 \times 13 = 5655$ ✓.
The larger number is **435**.
practice.shortcut: Multiply the HCF by the bigger 'other factor': 29 × 15 = 435. (5655 is the LCM, not a number.)

practice.q: Three pieces of timber 825 cm, 675 cm and 450 cm long have to be cut into planks of equal length. What is the greatest length of a plank that can measure all three exactly, and how many planks result in total?
practice.solution:
Greatest length $= \gcd(825, 675, 450) = 75$ cm.
Number of planks $= \frac{825 + 675 + 450}{75} = \frac{1950}{75} = 26$.
practice.shortcut: HCF is 75 (both 675 and 450 end in 75-multiples). Planks = total length ÷ 75 = 26.

practice.q: Find the greatest number of four digits which is exactly divisible by 15, 20 and 25.
practice.solution:
LCM$(15, 20, 25) = 300$.
Greatest four-digit number = 9999; $9999 \div 300$ leaves remainder 99.
Answer $= 9999 - 99 = 9900$.

practice.q: The product of two numbers is 2028 and their HCF is 13. How many pairs of such numbers are possible?
practice.solution:
Let the numbers be $13a$ and $13b$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$.
$13a \times 13b = 2028$ ⇒ $169ab = 2028$ ⇒ $ab = 12$.
Co-prime factor pairs of 12: $(1, 12)$ and $(3, 4)$.
Pairs of numbers: (13, 156) and (39, 52) ⇒ **2 pairs**.
practice.shortcut: product ÷ HCF² = 12 = 1×12 = 3×4 (co-prime only) ⇒ 2 pairs. (Answer 3 forgets the co-prime check: 2×6 shares a factor.)
practice.pattern: count pairs from product and HCF

practice.q: Find the least number of five digits which is exactly divisible by 32, 36, 40, 45 and 48.
practice.solution:
LCM $= 2^5 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 1440$.
$10000 \div 1440$ gives remainder 1360, so $1440 - 1360 = 80$ more is needed.
Answer $= 10000 + 80 = 10080$.
practice.shortcut: LCM 1440; step 10000 up to the next multiple: 7 × 1440 = 10080.

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 3, 4 and 5 leaves remainders 2, 3 and 4 respectively.
practice.solution:
In each case the remainder is 1 less than the divisor: N + 1 is divisible by 3, 4 and 5.
LCM$(3, 4, 5) = 60$ ⇒ N + 1 is a multiple of 60.
Least value: $N = 60 - 1 = 59$.
practice.shortcut: Remainder = divisor − 1 ⇒ N = LCM − 1 = 59.

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 6, 7, 8, 9 and 12 leaves a remainder of 1 in each case, and is exactly divisible by 13.
practice.solution:
N = LCM$(6,7,8,9,12)k + 1 = 504k + 1$.
Need $504k + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}$. Since $504 = 13 \times 38 + 10$, $10k \equiv -1 \equiv 12 \pmod{13}$.
$10k \equiv 12$ ⇒ multiply by 4: $40k \equiv 48$ ⇒ $k \equiv 9 \pmod{13}$ (since $40 \equiv 1$, $48 \equiv 9$).
Least $k = 9$: $N = 504 \times 9 + 1 = 4537$. Check: $4537 \div 13 = 349$ ✓.

practice.q: The HCF of $\frac{2}{3}$, $\frac{8}{9}$ and $\frac{10}{27}$ is:
practice.shortcut: HCF of tops = 2; LCM of bottoms = 27 ⇒ 2/27.

practice.q: The HCF of 0.54, 1.8 and 7.2 is:
practice.solution:
Write all with two decimal places: 0.54, 1.80, 7.20.
$\gcd(54, 180, 720) = 18$ ⇒ HCF $= 0.18$.
practice.shortcut: Clear decimals (×100): gcd(54, 180, 720) = 18, shift the point back → 0.18.

practice.q: What is the HCF of 72 and 120?
practice.solution:
$72 = 2^3 \times 3^2$, $120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5$.
Common primes with lowest powers: $2^3 \times 3 = 24$.
practice.shortcut: Both divide by 24: $72 = 3 \times 24$, $120 = 5 \times 24$; nothing bigger does.

practice.q: What is the LCM of 16, 24 and 36?
practice.shortcut: 72 uses $2^3$ (one 2 short); 288 is a common multiple but not the least.

practice.q: The HCF of two numbers is 18 and their LCM is 378. If one number is 54, find the other number.
practice.solution:
$\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = a \times b$ → other $= \frac{18 \times 378}{54} = 126$.
Check: $\gcd(54, 126) = 18$ and LCM$(54, 126) = 378$ ✓.

practice.q: The product of two numbers is 2160 and their HCF is 12. Find their LCM.
practice.solution:
$\text{LCM} = \frac{\text{product}}{\text{HCF}} = \frac{2160}{12} = 180$.
Check: 180 is a multiple of the HCF 12 ✓.

practice.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 3 : 4 and their HCF is 6. Find the sum of the numbers.
practice.solution:
Numbers: $3 \times 6 = 18$ and $4 \times 6 = 24$. Sum $= 42$.
(Their LCM is $6 \times 3 \times 4 = 72$.)
practice.shortcut: Sum = HCF × (sum of ratio parts) = 6 × 7 = 42.

practice.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 5 : 7 and their LCM is 140. Find the difference between the numbers.
practice.solution:
$\text{LCM} = h \times 5 \times 7 = 35h = 140$ → $h = 4$.
Numbers: 20 and 28 → difference $= 8$.

practice.q: The HCF of two numbers is 23 and the other two factors of their LCM are 13 and 14. Find the greater number.
practice.solution:
Numbers: $23 \times 13 = 299$ and $23 \times 14 = 322$.
Their LCM is $23 \times 13 \times 14 = 4186$ ✓. Greater number $= 322$.
practice.shortcut: 4186 is the LCM, not a number; 299 is the smaller one.

practice.q: The HCF of two numbers is 17 and the other two factors of their LCM are 11 and 13. Find the greater number.
practice.solution:
Numbers: $17 \times 11 = 187$ and $17 \times 13 = 221$ (11 and 13 are co-prime).
Greater number $= 221$. The LCM is $17 \times 11 \times 13 = 2431$.

practice.q: The LCM of two co-prime numbers is 221. If one of them is 13, find the other number.
practice.solution:
Co-prime numbers have HCF 1, so LCM = product.
Other number $= \frac{221}{13} = 17$.

practice.q: Which one of the following pairs of numbers is co-prime?
practice.solution:
Co-prime means HCF = 1.
$\gcd(14, 21) = 7$, $\gcd(27, 36) = 9$, $\gcd(30, 48) = 6$, but $\gcd(16, 25) = 1$.
So 16 and 25 are co-prime.
practice.shortcut: Two numbers need not both be prime to be co-prime — 16 and 25 are not prime, yet share no factor.

practice.q: Find the HCF of 135 and 225 using the division method.
practice.solution:
$225 = 1 \times 135 + 90$; $135 = 1 \times 90 + 45$; $90 = 2 \times 45 + 0$.
Last non-zero divisor $= 45$.

practice.q: Find the HCF of 4052 and 12576.
Find the HCF of 96, 240 and 384.
Find the HCF of $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5^4$, $2^2 \times 3^3 \times 5^2$ and $2^4 \times 3 \times 5^3$.
practice.solution:
Take each prime at its lowest power across the three numbers:
$2^2$ (lowest of 3, 2, 4), $3^1$ (lowest of 2, 3, 1), $5^2$ (lowest of 4, 2, 3).
HCF $= 4 \times 3 \times 25 = 300$.
practice.shortcut: 900 picks $3^2$ — but the third number has only $3^1$.

practice.q: Find the LCM of $2^3 \times 3^2$ and $2 \times 3^4$.
practice.solution:
Highest powers: $2^3$ and $3^4$.
LCM $= 8 \times 81 = 648$.
practice.shortcut: 216 = $2^3 \times 3^3$ takes the wrong (lower) power of 3.

practice.q: The HCF of two numbers is $2^3 \times 3$ and their LCM is $2^5 \times 3^3 \times 5$. If one number is $2^3 \times 3 \times 5$, find the other number.
practice.solution:
Other $= \frac{\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM}}{\text{given number}} = \frac{(2^3 \times 3) \times (2^5 \times 3^3 \times 5)}{2^3 \times 3 \times 5} = 2^5 \times 3^3 = 864$.
Check: $\gcd(120, 864) = 24$ ✓ and LCM$(120, 864) = 4320$ ✓.

practice.q: Find the LCM of $\frac{4}{9}$ and $\frac{10}{21}$.
practice.solution:
LCM of numerators: $\text{LCM}(4, 10) = 20$. HCF of denominators: $\gcd(9, 21) = 3$.
LCM $= \frac{20}{3}$.
Check: $\frac{20}{3} \div \frac{4}{9} = 15$ ✓ and $\frac{20}{3} \div \frac{10}{21} = 14$ ✓ — both whole.
practice.shortcut: Trap $\frac{40}{63}$ divides the LCM of tops by the LCM of bottoms — the bottoms need the HCF.

practice.q: Find the HCF of $\frac{8}{9}$, $\frac{16}{27}$ and $\frac{20}{81}$.
practice.solution:
HCF of numerators: $\gcd(8, 16, 20) = 4$. LCM of denominators: $\text{LCM}(9, 27, 81) = 81$.
HCF $= \frac{4}{81}$.

practice.q: Find the LCM of 0.12, 0.18 and 0.30.
practice.solution:
Clear decimals (× 100): 12, 18, 30 → LCM $= 180$.
Two decimal places → answer $= 1.80$.
Check: $1.8 \div 0.12 = 15$, $1.8 \div 0.18 = 10$, $1.8 \div 0.30 = 6$ — all whole ✓.

practice.q: Find the HCF of 1.44, 3.6 and 0.72.
practice.solution:
Clear decimals (× 100): 144, 360, 72 → $\gcd = 72$.
Restore two decimal places → HCF $= 0.72$.
Check: $1.44 \div 0.72 = 2$, $3.6 \div 0.72 = 5$, $0.72 \div 0.72 = 1$ ✓.
practice.shortcut: 0.36 also divides all three, but the HCF must be the greatest such number.

practice.q: Find the greatest number which divides 43, 91 and 183 leaving the same remainder 3 in each case.
practice.shortcut: Trap 8: it divides 40 and 88 but not 180 — check all three numbers.

practice.q: Find the greatest number which divides 82, 150 and 233 leaving remainders 4, 7 and 12 respectively.
practice.solution:
Subtract the remainders: $82 - 4 = 78$, $150 - 7 = 143$, $233 - 12 = 221$.
$78 = 6 \times 13$, $143 = 11 \times 13$, $221 = 17 \times 13$ → HCF $= 13$ (greater than every remainder ✓).

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 8, 12, 15 and 20 leaves a remainder of 4 in each case.
Find the least number greater than 10000 which when divided by 15, 18, 24 and 30 leaves a remainder of 9 in each case.
practice.solution:
LCM$(15, 18, 24, 30) = 360$ → numbers are $360k + 9$.
$27 \times 360 + 9 = 9729$ (too small); $28 \times 360 + 9 = 10089$ ✓.
Check: $10080$ is divisible by all four, so 10089 leaves 9 each time ✓.
practice.shortcut: 9731 fits the pattern but is below 10000; 10080 leaves remainder 0.

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 6, 9 and 12 leaves remainders 5, 8 and 11 respectively.
practice.solution:
Each remainder is 1 less than its divisor → N + 1 is divisible by 6, 9 and 12.
LCM $= 36$ → N $= 36 - 1 = 35$.
Check: $35 = 5 \times 6 + 5 = 3 \times 9 + 8 = 2 \times 12 + 11$ ✓.

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 7, 8 and 9 leaves remainders 5, 6 and 7 respectively.
practice.solution:
Each remainder is 2 less than its divisor → N + 2 is divisible by 7, 8 and 9.
LCM$(7, 8, 9) = 504$ → N $= 504 - 2 = 502$.
Check: $502 = 71 \times 7 + 5 = 62 \times 8 + 6 = 55 \times 9 + 7$ ✓.

practice.q: Three runners start together on a circular track, completing one lap in 12, 18 and 24 minutes respectively. After how many minutes will they be together at the starting point again?
practice.solution:
They meet at the start after a common multiple of 12, 18 and 24 minutes.
LCM $= 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72$ minutes.
practice.shortcut: 36 fails: $36 \div 24$ is not a whole number of laps for the third runner.

practice.q: Six bells commence tolling together and then toll at intervals of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 seconds. In 30 minutes, how many times do they toll together, counting the toll at the very start?
practice.solution:
LCM$(2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) = 120$ s $= 2$ min.
In 30 min there are $\frac{30}{2} = 15$ coincidences **after** the start; counting the start itself → $15 + 1 = 16$.

practice.q: What is the capacity of the largest vessel which can fill containers of 144 litres, 180 litres and 240 litres an exact number of times? Also, how many such fills empty the 240-litre container?
practice.solution:
Largest vessel $= \gcd(144, 180, 240) = 12$ litres.
Fills for the 240 L container: $240 \div 12 = 20$.

practice.q: Two rods measure 12 m 60 cm and 7 m 20 cm. They are cut into pieces of equal length, the length being the greatest possible. Find the length of a piece and the total number of pieces.
practice.solution:
In centimetres: 1260 and 720. Greatest length $= \gcd(1260, 720) = 180$ cm $= 1$ m 80 cm.
Total pieces $= \frac{1260 + 720}{180} = \frac{1980}{180} = 11$ (7 from the long rod + 4 from the short one).
practice.shortcut: 90 cm and 60 cm also measure both rods exactly, but the question wants the greatest length.

practice.q: A hall 12 m 96 cm long and 8 m 32 cm broad is to be paved with the least number of square tiles of the same size. Find the number of tiles.
practice.solution:
In centimetres: 1296 × 832. Largest tile side $= \gcd(1296, 832) = 16$ cm.
Tiles $= \frac{1296 \times 832}{16 \times 16} = 81 \times 52 = 4212$.
practice.shortcut: Convert metres to centimetres first — skipping that gives nonsense options.

practice.q: Find the greatest number of five digits which is exactly divisible by 42, 63 and 84.
practice.solution:
LCM$(42, 63, 84) = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7 = 252$.
$99999 \div 252$ leaves remainder 207 → greatest multiple $= 99999 - 207 = 99792$.
Check: $99792 = 396 \times 252$ ✓.
practice.shortcut: 99540 and 99288 are earlier multiples of 252 — not the greatest.

practice.q: Find the least four-digit number which when divided by 9, 12 and 16 leaves a remainder of 3 in each case.
practice.solution:
LCM$(9, 12, 16) = 144$ → numbers are $144k + 3$.
$6 \times 144 + 3 = 867$ (three digits); $7 \times 144 + 3 = 1011$ ✓.
Check: $1008$ is divisible by all three, so 1011 leaves remainder 3 each time ✓.
practice.shortcut: 1003 is 1000 + 3 — it ignores the LCM structure.

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 4, 6 and 9 leaves a remainder of 1 in each case, and which is exactly divisible by 11.
practice.shortcut: 109 also leaves remainder 1 each time but is not divisible by 11.

practice.q: Find the greatest number of five digits which when divided by 8, 12 and 16 leaves a remainder of 3 in each case.
practice.solution:
LCM$(8, 12, 16) = 48$; $99999 = 2083 \times 48 + 15$ → greatest multiple of 48 is 99984.
Answer $= 99984 + 3 = 99987$.
Check: $99984$ is divisible by all three, so 99987 leaves 3 each time ✓.
practice.shortcut: 99939 is 48 less — valid but not the greatest.

practice.q: The HCF and LCM of two numbers are 6 and 72 respectively. If their sum is 42, find their difference.
practice.solution:
Numbers are $6a$ and $6b$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ and $ab = \frac{72}{6} = 12$.
Co-prime pairs of 12: (1, 12) → numbers 6, 72 (sum 78); (3, 4) → numbers 18, 24 (sum 42 ✓).
Difference $= 24 - 18 = 6$.
practice.shortcut: 42 is the sum, not the difference — read the question again.

practice.q: The HCF and LCM of two numbers are 13 and 455 respectively. If one number lies between 60 and 80, find that number.
practice.solution:
$ab = \frac{455}{13} = 35$ → co-prime pairs (1, 35) and (5, 7).
Numbers: (13, 455) or (65, 91). Only 65 lies between 60 and 80 ✓.

practice.q: The product of two numbers is 2160 and their HCF is 12. How many pairs of such numbers are possible?
practice.solution:
Numbers are $12a$ and $12b$ with $ab = \frac{2160}{144} = 15$.
Co-prime factor pairs of 15: (1, 15) and (3, 5) → **2 pairs**: (12, 180) and (36, 60).
practice.shortcut: Answer 3 or 4 usually forgets the co-prime check — e.g. ab = 15 has only these two.

practice.q: The HCF and LCM of two numbers are 4 and 120 respectively. How many different pairs of such numbers are possible?
Find the greatest number which divides 70, 110 and 150 leaving the same remainder in each case. What is that remainder?
practice.solution:
Pairwise differences: $110 - 70 = 40$, $150 - 110 = 40$, $150 - 70 = 80$.
HCF of differences $= 40$. Remainder $= 70 \bmod 40 = 30$ (same for 110 and 150 ✓).

practice.q: Find the greatest number which divides 84, 156 and 204 leaving the same remainder in each case.
practice.solution:
Pairwise differences: $156 - 84 = 72$, $204 - 156 = 48$, $204 - 84 = 120$.
HCF$(72, 48, 120) = 24$; the common remainder is $84 \bmod 24 = 12$ ✓.
